Response to Reviewers
First of all, we sincerely thank the editor and reviewers for their time to read the manuscript and
for their effort to provide valuable and constructive feedback. All the comments and suggestions
are to the point and have helped us significantly improve the manuscript. Below, we provide a
point-by-point response to the comments raised. The original reviewers’ comments are in italics,
our replies in normal fonts and the changes to the manuscript in blue. Changes in the marked
version of the submitted revised manuscript are also highlighted in blue.
In particular, we carried out additional experiments on the photon correlation at different laser
repetition rates, and on the time evolution of single superlattice PL spectra. Further, we carried out
analysis of the photon bunching dynamics which provided us with the biexciton – exciton lifetime.
Based on this we reorganized the discussion part to strengthen the biexciton model proposed to
explain the observed phenomena.
We believe that the revised version sufficiently addresses all reviewers’ concerns, and we hope
that it now meets the standards for publication in Nature Communications. Detailed answers to the
individual comments are provided below.
Reviewer #1
Tan et al. report on the optical properties of self-assembled perovskite QD superlattices at room
temperature and observe collective blinking and bunched photon statistics, which are the key
results of the study. The origin of the collective behavior is attributed to exciton migration followed
by emission through the exciton-biexciton cascade. Considering the potential utility of this
material system for a variety of applications, this study presents phenomena and proposed
mechanisms that will be important for future work in this material system. Overall, the manuscript
is well written, clear, and cites relevant literature. However, in its present form, I don’t recommend
publication in Nature Communications.
We thank the reviewer for taking interest in our work.
In particular, the following points need to be addressed:
1. The power-dependence of the biexciton emission should increase quadratically at low power
(see ref. [61] Nano Lett. 16, 2349-2362 2016), but the data shown in Fig. 4(c) shows a linear
increase. This apparent discrepancy needs to be addressed.
The quadratic increase of biexciton emission in ref. [67,74,75] is caused by direct formation of
biexcitons by two-photon absorption. In contrast, here we put forward a model in which one-
photon absorption creates single excitons which then migrate to an emission center where the
increased exciton density leads to the formation of biexcitons via attractive interaction. As such,
the power dependence reflects the one-photon absorption process and increases linearly.
We rearranged the description of the model on page 11 to emphasize this point.
2. The authors also use the saturation behavior in Fig. 4(c) as evidence of biexciton emission.
However, both exciton and biexciton emission exhibit saturation behavior in ref. [67]. Can the
authors provide more detail on why they expect the emission from biexcitons to saturate, but not
excitons?
Thank you for this comment which lead us to reconsider the interpretation of the power
dependences. It is not the emission from biexcitons only but the total emission that saturates.
In
ref. [67], the onset of saturation of the emission from single excitons is close to N = 1. In our
experiment on single QDs (Fig. 4b) the onset of PL saturation shows around the 100 W/cm2
intensities, corresponding to N = 0. 75. However, for a typical superlattice containing 1000
individual QDs, the number N under 1 W/cm2 excitation is 7.5. Most of these excitons are funneled
to and accumulate in the emission center, where the resulting N is higher than the onset of
saturation. On the other hand, such funneling is not present in the random QD ensemble where
individual QDs emit independently and the linearity is maintained.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
3. Similarly, biexciton emission should result in a faster component to the PL emission lifetime
(see ref. [67] and many other studies across different material systems), but the authors report an
extended lifetime that they attribute (as far as I can tell) to the exciton migration to an emitting
site. It seems that this would result in delayed emission followed by fast emission rather than what
is observed. A quantitative model (e.g., Monte-Carlo with rate- equation modeling) of the proposed
emission process is important to confirm the proposed emission mechanisms.
PL emission lifetime of biexcitons mostly reflects the Auger recombination lifetime, and lifetime
values ranging from tens to hundreds of ps have been reported (in ref. [67, 70, 77] and elsewhere).
We have not resolved such short components in our experiments. However, in our photon
correlation experiments we are concerned with the mechanism of cascade-like biexciton-exciton
emission. Analysis of the photon bunching dynamics can in principle provide information on the
cascade-like process [84]. Specifically, fitting of the central 𝑔(2)(𝜏) peak and comparison with the
fitting of the side peaks enables extraction of a fast component which corresponds to the time delay
between the emission of the first (biexciton) and second (exciton) photons in the biexciton-exciton
cascade, and can be interpreted as the biexciton-exciton emission lifetime. We carried out such
analysis on the 𝑔(2)(𝜏) of several superlattices, and present an example in the Fig. 4d. The central
peak is well fit with a two-exponential function with lifetimes of 1.3 ns and 27 ns, respectively.
The side peaks show single exponential decay with a lifetime of 27 ns. We can therefore attribute
the 1.3 ns component to the biexciton-exciton delay (or biexciton lifetime). We note that the 1.3
ns value is very likely resolution-limited, and that the actual delay is shorter.
The fitting has been added as Fig. 4d and the above discussion including ref [84] added on page
12.
4. It would be useful, particularly for the readers of Nature Communications, to connect with a
broader community by referencing other material systems (e.g., epitaxial quantum dots, molecules,
defects in materials, colloidal nanocrystals). Some of these materials are more developed as
quantum light sources (including demonstrations of collective effects) and have also had
significant research devoted to exciton/biexciton dynamics.
We appreciate this suggestion and added a note in the introduction, including 3 representative
references.
A note on page 2 ad references [1-3] have been added.
5. The supplement has 11 figures, some without any description (aside from the brief description
in the main text). More detail describing the importance of the data shown is required.
We agree, the description of the figures has been expanded.
Minor comments:
Line 31 (and at various places in the text): It would be better to use more precise language (i.e.,
bunching with a g^((2) ) (0) up to 2.75).
Thank you, we corrected the expressions.
Line 88: Awkward phrasing (“Such and other requirements…”). Alternative: “These results…”.
Also, references to “other results” should be included, or the phrase shouldn’t be used.
Corrected, thank you.
Reviewer #2
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is
part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide
appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
We thank the reviewer for using this occasion for rigorous peer-review training of young
researchers which is very important for the future of science.
Reviewer #3
In this manuscript, Tan et al. demonstrate the fabrication of CsPbBr3 superlattices and their
unique optical properties with potential applications in quantum light generation for quantum
photonic technologies. First, the authors present the synthesis of CsPbBr3 QDs and their self-
assembly into CsPbBr3 superlattices. The ~10 nm cubic CsPbBr3 QDs self-assemble in a toluene
rich environment to make 100-500 nm-sized superlattices on a glass substrate. These CsPbBr3
superlattices exhibit emergent optical properties compared to a random ensemble of CsPbBr3
QDs, including narrower emission linewidths, longer emission lifetimes, multi-level blinking
behavior, and photon bunching. The degree of photon bunching and emission lifetime modification
varies superlattice-to-superlattice, as well as with the superlattice blinking intensity. Additionally,
a fluorescence lifetime intensity distribution (FLID) analysis was employed. The authors conclude
the FLID map suggests blinking results from the charging of the superlattices. Super-resolution
imaging was used to show that the emission is spatially confined to regions tens of nanometers in
size, suggesting excitation migration to localized energy traps. The authors argue that the
increased exciton density at these traps leads to higher biexciton formation rates. The combined
mechanism of exciton migration and biexciton formation results in the observed bunching
behavior and longer lifetimes in the CsPbBr3 superlattices.
While the observation of coherent superlattice blinking along with photon bunching is indeed an
unexpected and impactful result, there are discrepancies within the model proposed by the author
which are not well addressed within the manuscript. Furthermore, the experimental techniques
used to identify photon bunching appear to be flawed. These concerns are detailed in the list below.
Finally, a key property of quantum light generation is photon indistinguishability which is related
to the exciton coherence time and exciton lifetime. To achieve high photon indistinguishability, the
coherence time and the lifetime must be on similar timescales. The emission linewidth (inversely
related to the coherence time) of these CsPbBr3 superlattices suggests that the coherence time is
many orders of magnitude faster than the lifetime, meaning indistinguishability is extremely low.
Therefore, the motivation provided for why the authors observations are impactful is lacking. For
these reasons, I believe that publication in any form is premature at this time.
We thank the reviewer for the overall evaluation and understanding of the manuscript. Regarding
the lifetime, the values presented in the manuscript (tens of ns) reflect mainly the long-distance
migration of single excitons. In the revised version we added analysis of the photon bunching
dynamics which can, in principle, provide information on the cascade-like biexciton-exciton
emission process [84]. Fitting of the central 𝑔(2)(𝜏) peak and comparison with the fitting of the
side peaks enables extraction of a fast component which can be interpreted as the biexciton-exciton
emission lifetime. Such biexciton lifetime has sub-ns values, and is thus closer to the coherence
time mentioned by the reviewer.
However, we would like to stress that our primary motivation is not to demonstrate a light source
of highly indistinguishable photons, but rather to report on the discovery of the room temperature
collective phenomena and offer explanation of these novel observations that may have
implications in future quantum light generation.
The fitting has been added as Fig. 4c and the above discussion added on page 12 including ref [84].
Specific Comments:
1) The experimental conditions of the cross-correlation (g2(t)) measurements appear to be
inconsistent with the assumptions and criteria presented when the method was initially derived in
three fundamental ways (DOI: 10.1021/nl104054t).
The excitation densities used to measure the biexciton-exciton correlations appear to be too high.
To ensure second-order correlations within the same excitation pulse are a result of a biexciton-
exciton cascade process, the excitation density should be low enough such that negligible
multiexcitons that are higher-order than the biexciton are generated. Even at an excitation density
N = 0.75, the number of triexcitons generated is 25% that of biexciton generation which will lead
to misinterpretations of the biexciton behavior in the QD superlattice system.
The value of N = 0.75 exciton/QD refers to the extreme power of 100 W/cm2 in the power
dependence in Fig. 4b. For the photon correlation experiments we typically use the power of 1
W/cm2 which results in N = 0.0075 exciton/QD. In addition, as mentioned in the reply to the
question 1 of Reviewer #1, we assume one-photon absorption creating single excitons (which then
migrate to an emission center and form biexcitons), leading to the linear power dependence in Fig.
4b. We do not see any deviation from the linearity which would indicate direct formation of
biexcitons or higher order multiexcitons.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
Relatedly, the authors do not make it clear if they measure the CsPbBr3 superlattices at similar
powers as single CsPbBr3 QDs, assuming similar excitation densities. The absorption cross-
section of the superlattices should scale with the number of QDs within the lattice. If the
superlattices are excited at similar powers as the single QD, the excitation density of the
superlattice system may be significantly underestimated in this study leading to many higher-order
multiexcitons being generated in this system, greatly complicating the picture of the excited system.
The authors should measure the absorption cross-section of the CsPbBr3 superlattices and
measure the correlations at low excitation densities such that minimal multiexcitons higher than
the biexciton are generated within the entire superlattice.
Thank you for pointing out this important aspect. Unfortunately, we are unable to directly measure
the absorption cross-section of individual superlattices because we do not know the size of a
particular superlattice emitting under the microscope. The size information has been obtained
independently using SEM, and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. Again, the superlattice is measured with the power of 1 W/cm2 corresponding to N =
0.0075 exciton/QD. This would result in N = 7.5 excitons per superlattice. However, we assume
here that the absorption proceeds spatially randomly within the superlattice and occurs
independently on individual QDs within the structure. Therefore, the predominant process is linear
absorption creating a randomly distributed ensemble of single exciton which then accumulate in
the emission center.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
The repetition rate of the laser should be slow enough such that the emissive system is guaranteed
to be in the ground state before the next excitation pulse. Otherwise, multiple
excitons/multiexcitons may be generated at a faster rate than Poissonian statistics predict,
breaking down the above-mentioned assumption of the biexciton-exciton correlation
measurement. With lifetimes as long as 69 ns, I would expect repetition rates of 1 MHz or lower
would be necessary to ensure the excited state fully decays within the excitation window. The
authors utilized repetition rates of 2.5 MHz and faster. The authors should either justify the validity
of their chosen repetition rates or repeat the measurements to conform with the assumptions of
the methodology.
Yes, this is another very important point. We carried out additional experiments using the
repetition rates of 1 MHz and 5 MHz, and the results show that the effect of photon bunching is
clearly observed at these two frequencies. The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 6.
The bunching experiment with 1 MHz rate is has been mentioned on page 5 and Supplementary
Fig. 6 has been added.
2) The resolution of the correlation figures throughout the paper are low. Each peak within the
g2(t) appears to have ~10-15 data points which is not sufficient to identify relevant features within
the correlations, such as bunching. Typically, correlations are binned with a similar resolution as
a lifetime (1 ns). The authors should work up the correlation data with a finer time resolution to
better resolve the bunching effects.
Again, thank you for pointing this out. We redraw all the data in the figures with the 1 ns resolution.
The Fig. 2, and Supplementary Figs. 5, 7, 8, 9 have been modified.
3) The authors do not report the concentration of the QD toluene solutions that are used to perform
the self-assembly. It is further unclear how, when they measure the emission of single CsPbBr3
superlattices, they ensure that the emission is from only one superlattice. The authors should
elucidate how they identify isolated superlattices in their spectroscopic methods. Additionally, if

The information on the concentration (2.29 x 10-7 mol/L ) has been added in the Methods section.
The individual superlattices are identified in wide-field imaging mode in the CCD fluorescence

The Methods section has been modified. The Supplementary Fig. 3 has been added and described

4) Some superlattices have irregular shapes as shown in Fig. S2. The authors should report what
percentage of the superlattices have this irregular shape. The authors should present widefield
TEM images of the films CsPbBr3 superlattices to confirm these distributions. The authors should
further explain how they confirm whether they are looking at an irregular shaped superlattice vs.
a cubic superlattice when measuring the emission from the superlattices.
We used SEM to characterize the superlattice shape as it proved difficult to grow larger numbers
of well separated superlattices directly on the TEM grids. We measured the shape in total of 20
particles, 9 of which (approximately 50 %) showed the regular cubic shapes. We added more data
in the SI in Supplementary Fig. 2. As mentioned above, the SEM and fluorescence experiments
are carried out independently and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. We therefore cannot directly relate the shape and the PL properties on individual
particles, and we base our results on the assumption that the (mostly) two-level blinking originates
from the cubic-shaped superlattices. Also, the irregular-shaped superlattices are significantly
larger that the regular ones, and as such emit with higher intensities and small (if any) degree of
bunching. We do not include such superlattices in the statistical analysis presented in the paper.
The Supplementary Fig. 2 has been replaced.
5) In Fig. 2, the authors filter the emission by intensity and categorize the high and low intensity
sections as the ON-state and grey-state emission, respectively. I would argue that the ON-state is
broader than is suggested by the filtering cut-off around 0.2 kc/ms, and is partially captured within
the grey-state. Because of this it appears possible that the grey-state is actually an OFF-state.
The authors should utilize a range of cutoffs to clearly demonstrate the presence of a grey state rather
than an artifact due to thresholding.
We agree that assigning the grey state based on the intensity level only can be ambiguous. Here,
we also confirmed that the grey state has PL lifetime characteristic of perovskite QDs, and based
on the suggestion of the reviewer #4 we also verified that the PL spectrum of the grey state
corresponds to the perovskite spectrum. None of these would be expected for completely OFF
state where the signal would be originating from background scattering or impurity fluorescence.
The classification of grey state has been added on page 4, 6 and 12.
6) On pg. 8, the authors suggest that the double Gaussian fit to the CsPbBr3 superlattice emission
spectrum (Fig. 4a) with an energy splitting of 23 meV is evidence of biexciton-exciton cascade
emission. It is difficult to believe in this evidence, because given the low excitation densities in
these measurements, biexciton emission should contribute less than 5% of the total emission,
before accounting for reduced emission efficiencies of multiexcitons due to Auger recombination.
The integrated intensities of the two Gaussians in the emission spectrum in Fig. 4a appear to have
approximately equal areas which would be unreasonable if the lower energy Gaussian was
biexciton emission. To the best of our knowledge, the prevailing wisdom within the community
ascribes the lower energy shoulder of the room temperature ensemble emission spectrum of
CsPbBr3 to the inelastic phonon scattering of optical phonons. The authors should provide more
evidence that the lower energy shoulder results from biexciton emission via power dependent
emission spectra.
We based our explanation of the PL spectral shape of the superlattices on the fact that neither the
random ensemble nor single QDs show the low-energy shoulder. We added examples of single
QD spectra in the SI (Supplementary Fig. 17), and these are characterized by mostly Lorentzian
lineshapes. Also, as we do not directly excite the biexcitons, the biexciton contribution can be
larger than the 5% the reviewer mentions, and would depend on the probability of the biexciton
formation in the emitting site. This interpretation is also not contradicted by the comparison of PL
spectra between the ON and grey states (measured upon the suggestion of the reviewer #4) which
shows that there is no difference between the two because the GREY state in many cases does
show bunching similar to the ON state. This is a consequence of the fact that (as mentioned in
the main text) the photon bunching and collective blinking are separate independently occurring
phenomena.
Given the above, we believe that the exciton binding energy is one of the plausible explanations
of the spectral shape. However, we admit that the contribution of the low-energy shoulder is
relatively high, and that other explanations might be possible, such as the exciton-phonon
coupling proposed by the reviewer. However, such phenomenon would have to be specific to the
superlattices as it is not observed for the constituting QDs.
The above discussion and Supplementary Fig. 17 have been added in the rearranged description
of the model on page 13.
7) As the authors show in Fig. S8, the strong antibunching in the g2(t) of a single CsPbBr3
indicates the biexciton quantum yield of single CsPbBr3 QDs is very low. However, the center
peak in the CsPbBr3 superlattice correlation is strongly bunched. These results appear entirely
contradictory. Since the biexciton quantum yield is low for single CsPbBr3 QDs, the authors need
to justify why formation of assemblies drastically changes the single QD multiexciton properties.
We agree that these results may appear initially counterintuitive. Our model assumes that even
though direct biexciton formation in individual QDs is very low (also because of the low excitation
intensity), the individual QDs in the superlatice work as an antenna and funnel individual excitons
into the emission center where the increased exciton density and attractive interaction lead to the
biexciton formation. We also note that in literature there has been nice demonstration of the
transition from antibunching to bunching when the number of coupled QDs increased from 1 to 3
[49]. Also, very recently both single-exciton anti-bunching and multiexciton bunching have been
demonstrated in single large perovskite nanocrystals [50].
The above point has been mentioned on page 6 and references [49,50] were added.
8) The authors show in Fig. 4c that the degree of bunching increases with decreasing PL intensity.
It is unclear why bunching would increase with lower PL intensities, and the authors do not
provide further explanation. At lower PL intensities, it is possible for background counts and/or
laser scatter to introduce artifacts in the correlations, artificially increasing or decreasing the
correlation contributions to the center peak. Given the concern of potential artifacts, the authors
should justify the anti-correlation of the bunching and PL intensity as it is unintuitive why this
behavior occurs.
This phenomenon of increasing degree of bunching with decreasing excitation power (Fig. 4a) has
been first observed on GaAs quantum dots [78], and later confirmed on InGaAs QDs [81], as
well as perovskites [10], and recently [50]. It is caused by the fact that at high excitation intensities
(high number of biexcitons) the probability of individual photon emission (from biexciton to
exciton) surpasses the correlated photon pair emission from the biexciton-exciton cascade. The
process has been theoretically described in the ref. [78] and we present the explanation in the
Supplementary information.
This discussion has been added on page 9.
Reviewer #4
(Remarks to the Author)
See attached pdf file.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their additional time and work spent on our
manuscript. We appreciate the reviewers’ honest effort to help improve the work. Below,
we provide a point-by-point response to the comments raised. We include only the new
comments that require further response. The original reviewers’ comments are in italics
grey, our previous replies in italics blue, the new comments on the revision in italics black,
our new responses in normal fonts and the changes to the manuscript in blue. Changes in the marked
version of the submitted revised manuscript are also highlighted in blue.
As part of the second revision we carried out further experiments to fully address the
reviewers’ comments, and added 7 new Supplementary figures. We believe that in the two
rounds of extensive revisions, both of which included substantial new experimental
evidence wherever required by the reviewers, we succeeded in addressing all the
reviewers’ criticism. Also, we provided further convincing arguments, based on
experimental facts, theoretical model, published literature and widely accepted consensus
in the field, to support our mechanism and interpretation of the phenomena, and to
alleviate the Reviewers’ concerns. We hope that the manuscript now meets the standards
for publication in Nature Communications. Detailed answers to the individual comments
are provided below.
Reviewer #1
I am satisfied with the responses to my comments, as well as the changes made to the
main text and supplement. I have also read through the other referee reports and find that
the authors have adequately addressed the concerns in their responses and through
corresponding changes to the manuscript.
Reviewer #3
Specific Comments:
1) The experimental conditions of the cross-correlation (g2(t)) measurements appear to
be inconsistent with the assumptions and criteria presented when the method was initially
derived in three fundamental ways (DOI: 10.1021/nl104054t). The excitation densities
used to measure the biexciton-exciton correlations appear to be too high. To ensure
second-order correlations within the same excitation pulse are a result of a biexciton-
exciton cascade process, the excitation density should be low enough such that negligible
multiexcitons that are higher-order than the biexciton are generated. Even at an
excitation density N = 0.75, the number of triexcitons generated is 25% that of biexciton
generation which will lead to misinterpretations of the biexciton behavior in the QD
superlattice system.
The value of N = 0.75 exciton/QD refers to the extreme power of 100 W/cm2 in the power
dependence in Fig. 4b. For the photon correlation experiments we typically use the power
of 1 W/cm2 which results in N = 0.0075 exciton/QD. In addition, as mentioned in the
reply to the question 1 of Reviewer #1, we assume one-photon absorption creating single
excitons (which then migrate to an emission center and form biexcitons), leading to the
linear power dependence in Fig. 4b. We do not see any deviation from the linearity which
would indicate direct formation of biexcitons or higher order multiexcitons.
Thank you for clarifying the fluences used in the excitation of single CsPbBr3
superlattices. Although the excitation density N = 0.0075/QD (assuming the absorption
cross-section scales linearly with the number of NCs in the superlattice) should primarily
lead to single exciton generation, the total excitation density N = 7.5 of single CsPbBr3
superlattices remains a serious concern. If the exciton funneling mechanism proposed by
the authors is true, then it is likely that there are many higher-order multiexcitons that
are formed as excitons funnel to emission centers. As the number of higher-order
multiexcitons present in the system increases, it becomes difficult to interpret the second
order cross-correlation measurement 𝑔(2)(𝜏). There is no way to distinguish a biexciton-exciton correlation from a triexciton-biexciton correlation from a triexciton-exciton
correlation (and so on). We do not believe it is reasonable to conclude that bunching is a
result of the biexciton-exciton cascade process while there are likely many higher-order
multiexcitons present in the system. Further studies should be performed at much lower
excitation densities (N < 0.1; N < 0.0001/QD) to ensure that there is a negligible
likelihood of three or more excitons present in the CsPbBr3 superlattice at any given time.
We understand the reviewer’s concern. The total exciton density of N = 7.5 per single
superlattice at 1 W/cm2 is an ideal estimate. Assuming a realistic value of PLQY of 80%,
this number would drop to N = 6, as 20% of the excitons would decay non-radiatively
before reaching the center. Further, on the funneling pathways from different parts of the
superlattice the actual density would be much smaller, meaning that higher-order
multiexcitons would unlikely form on the way to the emission center. To obtain more
experimental evidence, we measured the bunching characteristics with 0.5 W/cm2, which
corresponds to N ~ 3 excitons (or 0.003 exciton/QD), as proposed by the reviewer. The
power of 0.5 W/cm2 represents the lowest possible limit of the excitation intensity to
obtain reliable 𝑔(2)(𝜏) data with reasonable S/N ratio. The result for the photon bunching
obtained on a superlattice at 0.5 W/cm2 and 1.0 W/cm2 excitation intensities are shown
as an example in the Supplementary Fig. 18. The superlattice shows significantly higher
degree of bunching for the lower intensity (2.07 vs 1.42). This result indicates that
increasing the intensity does not create more multiexcitons that would contribute to the
increase in bunching (such multiexciton-induced increase in bunching with excitation
intensity was reported, e.g., in [PRL 94, 087403 (2005)]), and that the trend is in very
good agreement with the Fig. 4a and Eq. (3), i.e., with the excitation power dependence
expected for biexciton cascade emission. The result thus fully confirms our proposed
model.
Description of the bunching at low excitation power and the above reference (as [84])
were added on page 9, and the Supplementary Fig. 18 was added in the SI.
2) The resolution of the correlation figures throughout the paper are low. Each peak
within the g2(t) appears to have ~10-15 data points which is not sufficient to identify
relevant features within the correlations, such as bunching. Typically, correlations are
binned with a similar resolution as a lifetime (1 ns). The authors should work up the
correlation data with a finer time resolution to better resolve the bunching effects.
Again, thank you for pointing this out. We redraw all the data in the figures with the 1 ns
resolution.
We appreciate the effort made to change the resolution of the correlation figures. The
added resolution enables further insight and analysis of the correlation dynamics. It is
interesting to see that the bunching effects are primarily within a small number of data
points in the center peak. Regarding Supplementary Fig. 6, is the degree of bunching of
1.3 calculated based on the ratio of the peak intensities, or the integrated areas of the
center and side peak?
The degree of bunching is based on the ratio of peak intensities.
We added this information in the Methods section.
4) Some superlattices have irregular shapes as shown in Fig. S2. The authors should
report what percentage of the superlattices have this irregular shape. The authors should
present widefield TEM images of the films CsPbBr3 superlattices to confirm these
distributions. The authors should further explain how they confirm whether they are
looking at an irregular shaped superlattice vs. a cubic superlattice when measuring the
emission from the superlattices.
We used SEM to characterize the superlattice shape as it proved difficult to grow larger
numbers of well separated superlattices directly on the TEM grids. We measured the
shape in total of 20 particles, 9 of which (approximately 50 %) showed the regular cubic
shapes. We added more data in the SI in Supplementary Fig. 2. As mentioned above, the
SEM and fluorescence experiments are carried out independently and correlating the two
techniques is beyond our experimental capabilities. We therefore cannot directly relate
the shape and the PL properties on individual particles, and we base our results on the
assumption that the (mostly) two-level blinking originates from the cubic-shaped superlattices.
Also, the irregular-shaped superlattices are significantly larger that the regular ones, and
as such emit with higher intensities and small (if any) degree of bunching. We do not
include such superlattices in the statistical analysis presented in the paper.
Thank you to the authors for providing additional information on the cubic vs. irregularly
shaped CsPbBr3 superlattice structures. The authors make a reasonable justification to
determine whether they are measuring the emission coming from a cubic vs. irregularly
shaped superlattice, however it would be helpful to the readers to understand roughly
how much brighter the irregularly shaped superlattices are compared to the cubic shaped
superlattices.
The maximum emission intensity of the multi-level blinking particles is about twice or
more than that of the two-level blinking particles.
This information was added in the description of Supplementary Fig. 2.
5) In Fig. 2, the authors filter the emission by intensity and categorize the high and low
intensity sections as the ON-state and grey-state emission, respectively. I would argue
that the ON-state is broader than is suggested by the filtering cut-off around 0.2 kc/ms,
and is partially captured within the grey-state. Because of this it appears possible that
the grey-state is actually an OFF state. The authors should utilize a range of cutoffs to
clearly demonstrate the presence of a grey state rather than an artifact due to thresholding.
We agree that assigning the grey state based on the intensity level only can be ambiguous.
Here, we also confirmed that the grey state has PL lifetime characteristic of perovskite
QDs, and based on the suggestion of the reviewer #4 we also verified that the PL spectrum
of the grey state corresponds to the perovskite spectrum. None of these would be expected
for completely OFF state where the signal would be originating from background
scattering or impurity fluorescence.
We want to thank the authors for their response. However, we don’t believe our initial
comment was addressed. We apologize if our initial comment was not clear so we will
attempt to restate it below. We were curious to know what the grey-state lifetime would
look like if the threshold was set at an even lower value such as 0.05 kc/ms (marked by
the black cutoff line in the below figure). We were initially concerned that some of the
ON-state was captured within the grey-state due to the arbitrarily created thresholding
value around 0.22 kc/ms. We have marked this value on Fig. 2a for clarity.
Thank you for suggesting this important confirmation. We re-analyzed the trace for ‘pure’
grey state (below 0.05 kc/ms) and for ‘pure’ ON-state (for 0.375 - 0.45 kc/ms). The data
are presented in the Supplementary Fig. 14, and show that there is no difference in the
lifetimes from the ON-states. The grey state does show slight shortening of the long
component from 22 ns to 18 ns. This means that there might be some ON-states admixed
with the grey state at the original 0.22 kc/ms threshold (as the reviewer proposed), but it
also shows that the intensity values below 0.05 kc/ms correspond to a true grey state and
not and OFF-state.
A note was added on page 6 and the Supplementary Fig. 14 was added in the SI.
The integrated intensities of the two Gaussians in the emission spectrum in Fig. 4a appear
to have approximately equal areas which would be unreasonable if the lower energy
Gaussian was biexciton emission. To the best of our knowledge, the prevailing wisdom
within the community ascribes the lower energy shoulder of the room temperature
ensemble emission spectrum of CsPbBr3 to the inelastic phonon scattering of optical
phonons. The authors should provide more evidence that the lower energy shoulder
results from biexciton emission via power dependent emission spectra.
We based our explanation of the PL spectral shape of the superlattices on the fact that
neither the random ensemble nor single QDs show the low-energy shoulder. We added
examples of single QD spectra in the SI (Supplementary Fig. 17), and these are
characterized by mostly Lorentzian lineshapes. Also, as we do not directly excite the
biexcitons, the biexciton contribution can be larger than the 5% the reviewer mentions,
and would depend on the probability of the biexciton formation in the emitting site. This
interpretation is also not contradicted by the comparison of PL spectra between the ON
and grey states (measured upon the suggestion of the reviewer #4) which shows that there
is no difference between the two because the GREY state in many cases does show
bunching similar to the ON state. This is a consequence of the fact that (as mentioned in
the main text) the photon bunching and collective blinking are separate independently
occurring phenomena. Given the above, we believe that the exciton binding energy is one
of the plausible explanations of the spectral shape. However, we admit that the
contribution of the low-energy shoulder is relatively high, and that other explanations
might be possible, such as the exciton-phonon coupling proposed by the reviewer.
However, such phenomenon would have to be specific to the superlattices as it is not
observed for the constituting QDs.
The above discussion and Supplementary Fig. 17 have been added in the rearranged description
of the model on page 13.
Thank you to the authors for their insightful response. The language added to the
manuscript acknowledges the various plausible explanations. In this context, it seems
reasonable to propose the biexciton binding energy as one of the possibilities. We will
note however, if we assume that biexciton formation is much higher than what I was
proposing in our initial comment (5% of total emission), then we have a similar concern
as stated in 1) regarding the exciton/multiexciton distribution in the single CsPbBr3
superlattices that have implications on the accurate interpretations of the 𝑔(2)(𝜏)
bunching experiments.
The multiexciton question was addressed in response to Comment 1).
7) As the authors show in Fig. S8, the strong antibunching in the g2(t) of a single CsPbBr3
indicates the biexciton quantum yield of single CsPbBr3 QDs is very low. However, the center
peak in the CsPbBr3 superlattice correlation is strongly bunched. These results appear
entirely contradictory. Since the biexciton quantum yield is low for single CsPbBr3 QDs,
the authors need to justify why formation of assemblies drastically changes the single QD
multiexciton properties.
We agree that these results may appear initially counterintuitive. Our model assumes that
even though direct biexciton formation in individual QDs is very low (also because of the
low excitation intensity), the individual QDs in the superlattice work as an antenna and
funnel individual excitons into the emission center where the increased exciton density
and attractive interaction lead to the biexciton formation. We also note that in literature
there has been nice demonstration of the transition from antibunching to bunching when
the number of coupled QDs increased from 1 to 3 [49]. Also, very recently both single-exciton anti-bunching and multiexciton bunching have been demonstrated in single large
perovskite nanocrystals [50].
Thank you to the authors for their response. We maintain concern about the mechanistic
conclusions of the bunching phenomenon observed in these CsPbBr3 superlattices for a
few reasons. First, references [10,49,50,78,81] are on coherent systems at cryogenic
temperatures (4 Kelvin) where indistinguishability of photon emission can be reasonably
achieved. Indistinguishability is attributed as a key property in order to achieve the
ladder-like emission that results in bunching. Reference [49] shows the difference in
bunching as 2 QDs are tuned in and out of indistinguishability. To our knowledge, photon
indistinguishability has never been demonstrated in any QD system at room temperature,
suggesting it is unlikely the CsPbBr3 superlattices undergo the same process to produce
bunched 𝑔(2)(𝜏) measurements. Second, the QD systems in references [49,50,78]
required specific engineering solutions to achieve indistinguishability, and therefore
bunching. For ref [49], the emission from the 3 coupled QDs were not intrinsically
indistinguishable. The emission energy was tuned via strain and electric field effects to
place the 3 QD emission energies in resonance with one another. For ref [50], the
single large perovskite nanocrystal size was tuned so that the biexciton-to-exciton transition
would be in resonance with the exciton-to-optical-phonon transition. Additionally, the
exciton emission and trion emission were filtered in order to observe bunching. For ref
[78], the Hanbury Brown Twiss 𝑔(2)(𝜏) spectroscopic setup was spectrally filtered such
that one detector only accepted biexciton emission and the other detector only accepted
exciton emission, leading to the bunching effect. If the spectroscopic setup was not
spectrally filtered, bunching would not be expected. The observed bunching on the
CsPbBr3 superlattices is extremely interesting, however I do not believe there is sufficient
evidence at this time to propose a precise mechanism of bunching. As shown in the
references cited by the authors, coherent ladder-like biexciton-exciton cascade requires
stringent design in other single quantum dot or small number of coupled quantum dot
systems at cryogenic temperatures. Therefore, it seems highly unlikely that the room
temperature CsPbBr3 superlattice (comprised of ~1000 coupled NCs) is undergoing a
coherent ladder-like emissive process that could result in the proposed bunching process.
We believe further investigation into the mechanism of bunching is required before
recommending publication.
The reviewer’s original question was that ‘… strong antibunching in the g2(t) of a single
CsPbBr3 indicates the biexciton quantum yield of single CsPbBr3 QDs is very low.
However, the center peak in the CsPbBr3 superlattice correlation is strongly bunched.
These results appear entirely contradictory.’ We replied to explain the contradiction and
reiterated that in our model direct biexciton formation in individual QDs maybe indeed
low but the superlattice works as an antenna and funnels the excitons into the emission
center where the increased exciton density and attractive interaction lead to the
biexciton formation. For illustration, we cited a few examples of literature that did show
transition from antibunching to bunching with increasing size, but by no means we meant
to imply that our phenomena are equivalent to those observed in the references. As the
reviewer notes, the low-temperature experiments required filtering or energy tuning because
of the clear separation of the exciton-biexciton spectra. At room temperature the two spectra
largely overlap, and filtering is not required. It might be that ‘photon indistinguishability has
never been demonstrated in any QD system at room temperature’, but ordered (ladder-
like) photon emission from multiexciton states of a QD at room-temperature measured
by photon correlation techniques has been reported more than 20 years ago and many
times since then. [PRL 94, 087403 (2005)]. This fact well supports our interpretation of
cascade-like biexciton emission.
We agree with the reviewer that it is unlikely that the whole CsPbBr3 superlattice
comprised of ~1000 coupled NCs would undergo coherent ladder-like emission at room
temperature, but that is not what we are claiming. Again, the whole superlattice functions
as an antenna and the emission originates from very small region in the superlattice. This
region may contain ~ 10 or less NCs, and the cascade-like emission is confined to this
well-ordered part of the superlattice. The strongest evidence for the cascade-like emission
is the excitation intensity dependence in Fig. 4a (and indirectly also the PL intensity
dependence in Fig. 2c). This dependence follows a theoretical model (derived by two
independent ways in the SI) that explains the trend based on the biexciton cascade-like
emission. To the best of our knowledge there is no other model that would explain
decrease of photon bunching with increasing excitation intensity. We would be of course
open to other interpretations of the photon bunching phenomenon, but so far found none
that would explain all the experimental observations; we also believe that our model of
the bunching mechanism is not contradicting any existing knowledge in the field.
Reviewer #4
In this study, Tan et al. report on observed collective blinking and photon bunching from
individual perovskite quantum dot superlattices. The Reviewer has previously suggested
that the paper has an issue in that two phenomena are observed: collective blinking and
photon bunching. Were both phenomena to be connected, this would be rather interesting.
However, the authors do not find a connection between them. Instead, separate studies
are done to try and explain observed blinking and bunching. The problem with this is that
there is a certain depth that would ideally be met so that both separate sub studies would
be deep and truly impactful. Unfortunately, the Reviewer is still of the opinion that this
bar has not been cleared.
Thank you for bringing up this aspect of the work that we have not sufficiently stressed
in the current version of the manuscript. The impression might be that the blinking and
photon bunching are two separate phenomena happening by coincidence on the same
superlattice, but they are in fact both deeply related via the presence of the confined
emission center. Both are manifestations and consequences of the antenna effect of the
superlattice and of funneling of the excitons to this center. The high density of the excitons
in the small confined area (comprising ~ 10 or less QDs) is then responsible for both the
collective blinking and the photon bunching.
We have not delved into the mechanism of blinking of CsPbBr as this has been
covered extensively in literature, and instead concentrated on describing the novel aspect
of the collective blinking. But we followed the reviewer’s recommendation and
elaborated more on the mechanism by examining the blinking at lower excitation
intensities. We believe that with respect to the photon bunching we carried out extensive
characterization of this novel observation on a perovskite superlattice, and put forward a
mechanism (including theoretical model) that succeeds in explaining all the experimental
data and is not contradicting any existing knowledge in the field.
We have rearranged and expanded the conclusion part as a Discussion section on
pages 13-14, and summarized our explanation of the phenomena, including the
relationship between the collective blinking and photon bunching.
Comment 1. The Reviewer would like the authors to provide more details of their
experiment. For example, what was the integration time of their EMCCD when acquiring
the trajectories being shown? What is the integration time in Figure 2a? If the integration
time can be lowered, then it might be interesting to observe what happens to the
appearance of the trajectory and whether the bimodal “ON” and “GREY” designations
still hold. This comment also applies to the cases where there are multiple “ON” states.
It also applies to the non-blinking superlattice in Figure S7. Presumably lowering the
integration time in Figure S7 would show that there are actually “GREY” periods.
Author Response: The integration times using the EMCCD camera were 30 ms, the times
using the APD were 10 ms. The blinking trace in Fig. 2a was obtained using the APD
with the 10 ms integration time. For both detectors these are practically the limiting
values, making it difficult to lower the integration time.
Reviewer new comment: The Reviewer understands that the authors are using a Picoharp
instrument. In this case, it is possible to run the experiment using time tagged time
resolved mode (TTTR) where each received photon is time stamped. Consequently, photon
trajectories can be constructed with arbitrary bin widths. For example, one can bin the
received photons with a 10 ms overall integration or a 30 ms integration etc… The
Reviewer therefore questions the authors assertion that 10 ms is a lower limit when using
their stated photon counting system.
The reviewer is absolutely correct and we apologize for the somewhat misleading
response. In the confocal mode we did use the TTTR acquisition mode, and the
HydraHarp software used for the analysis enables integration times as short as 0.2 ms. In
the Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25 we re-analyzed two of the original blinking traces
using several integration times. It is clear that with the shorter times (< 2 ms), the
individual intensity levels in the histogram get smeared out due to the increased noise. At
the same time, shortening of the bin time did not reveal any additional features such as
unresolved OFF or grey states. We therefore used the 10 ms bin as the optimum
compromise between the S/N ratio and the resolution.
This explanation was added in the Methods section on page 15, and the Supplementary
Figs. 24 and 25 were added in the SI.
Comment 2. Related to this, the Reviewer requests that the authors explicitly state the
excitation intensities used to acquire all blinking trajectories. Additionally, (1) the
authors should state how superlattices are excited. Are they being illuminated as a whole
(illumination covers the entire superlattice) or does the laser focus to the center of the
superlattice. In short, report the spot size of the laser. (2) What do trajectories look like
at lower excitation intensities? Do they show say more “GREY” behavior? Or do they
look self-similar at all excitation intensities.
Author response: The excitation intensity was kept at 1 W/cm2 for all data throughout the
manuscript except the excitation intensity dependence. The PL lifetime and photon
correlation experiments were carried out in confocal mode with the laser diameter of
approximately 500 nm. For imaging and spectroscopy a wide-field fluorescence mode
was used. We have not specifically looked into the intensity dependence of the blinking
traces. We do have some data for 0.7 W/cm2 excitation which look similar but it is difficult
to make any conclusions due to the lack of statistics.
Reviewer new comment: The Reviewer would still prefer that the authors analyze their
blinking behavior at different excitation intensities, especially lower intensities. This is
because GREY states are suggested to be due to positively or negatively charged trions.
It would therefore seem that one way to indirectly test for this is to establish that the

We followed the Reviewer’s suggestion and analyzed blinking data for a series of

The Supplementary Fig. 17 and its description were added on page 8.
