size, suggesting excitation migration to localized energy traps. The authors argue that the
increased exciton density at these traps leads to higher biexciton formation rates. The combined
mechanism of exciton migration and biexciton formation results in the observed bunching
behavior and longer lifetimes in the CsPbBr3 superlattices.
While the observation of coherent superlattice blinking along with photon bunching is indeed an
unexpected and impactful result, there are discrepancies within the model proposed by the author
which are not well addressed within the manuscript. Furthermore, the experimental techniques
used to identify photon bunching appear to be flawed. These concerns are detailed in the list below.
Finally, a key property of quantum light generation is photon indistinguishability which is related
to the exciton coherence time and exciton lifetime. To achieve high photon indistinguishability, the
coherence time and the lifetime must be on similar timescales. The emission linewidth (inversely
related to the coherence time) of these CsPbBr3 superlattices suggests that the coherence time is
many orders of magnitude faster than the lifetime, meaning indistinguishability is extremely low.
Therefore, the motivation provided for why the authors observations are impactful is lacking. For
these reasons, I believe that publication in any form is premature at this time.
We thank the reviewer for the overall evaluation and understanding of the manuscript. Regarding
the lifetime, the values presented in the manuscript (tens of ns) reflect mainly the long-distance
migration of single excitons. In the revised version we added analysis of the photon bunching
dynamics which can, in principle, provide information on the cascade-like biexciton-exciton
emission process [84]. Fitting of the central 𝑔(2)(𝜏) peak and comparison with the fitting of the
side peaks enables extraction of a fast component which can be interpreted as the biexciton-exciton
emission lifetime. Such biexciton lifetime has sub-ns values, and is thus closer to the coherence
time mentioned by the reviewer.
However, we would like to stress that our primary motivation is not to demonstrate a light source
of highly indistinguishable photons, but rather to report on the discovery of the room temperature
collective phenomena and offer explanation of these novel observations that may have
implications in future quantum light generation.
The fitting has been added as Fig. 4c and the above discussion added on page 12 including ref [84].
Specific Comments:
1) The experimental conditions of the cross-correlation (g2(t)) measurements appear to be
inconsistent with the assumptions and criteria presented when the method was initially derived in
three fundamental ways (DOI: 10.1021/nl104054t).
The excitation densities used to measure the biexciton-exciton correlations appear to be too high.
To ensure second-order correlations within the same excitation pulse are a result of a biexciton-
exciton cascade process, the excitation density should be low enough such that negligible
multiexcitons that are higher-order than the biexciton are generated. Even at an excitation density
N = 0.75, the number of triexcitons generated is 25% that of biexciton generation which will lead
to misinterpretations of the biexciton behavior in the QD superlattice system.
The value of N = 0.75 exciton/QD refers to the extreme power of 100 W/cm2 in the power
dependence in Fig. 4b. For the photon correlation experiments we typically use the power of 1
W/cm2 which results in N = 0.0075 exciton/QD. In addition, as mentioned in the reply to the
question 1 of Reviewer #1, we assume one-photon absorption creating single excitons (which then
migrate to an emission center and form biexcitons), leading to the linear power dependence in Fig.
4b. We do not see any deviation from the linearity which would indicate direct formation of
biexcitons or higher order multiexcitons.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
Relatedly, the authors do not make it clear if they measure the CsPbBr3 superlattices at similar
powers as single CsPbBr3 QDs, assuming similar excitation densities. The absorption cross-
section of the superlattices should scale with the number of QDs within the lattice. If the
superlattices are excited at similar powers as the single QD, the excitation density of the
superlattice system may be significantly underestimated in this study leading to many higher-order
multiexcitons being generated in this system, greatly complicating the picture of the excited system.
The authors should measure the absorption cross-section of the CsPbBr3 superlattices and
measure the correlations at low excitation densities such that minimal multiexcitons higher than
the biexciton are generated within the entire superlattice.
Thank you for pointing out this important aspect. Unfortunately, we are unable to directly measure
the absorption cross-section of individual superlattices because we do not know the size of a
particular superlattice emitting under the microscope. The size information has been obtained
independently using SEM, and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. Again, the superlattice is measured with the power of 1 W/cm2 corresponding to N =
0.0075 exciton/QD. This would result in N = 7.5 excitons per superlattice. However, we assume
here that the absorption proceeds spatially randomly within the superlattice and occurs
independently on individual QDs within the structure. Therefore, the predominant process is linear
absorption creating a randomly distributed ensemble of single exciton which then accumulate in
the emission center.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
The repetition rate of the laser should be slow enough such that the emissive system is guaranteed
to be in the ground state before the next excitation pulse. Otherwise, multiple
excitons/multiexcitons may be generated at a faster rate than Poissonian statistics predict,
breaking down the above-mentioned assumption of the biexciton-exciton correlation measurement.
With lifetimes as long as 69 ns, I would expect repetition rates of 1 MHz or lower would be
necessary to ensure the excited state fully decays within the excitation window. The authors utilized
repetition rates of 2.5 MHz and faster. The authors should either justify the validity of their chosen
repetition rates or repeat the measurements to conform with the assumptions of the methodology.
Yes, this is another very important point. We carried out additional experiments using the
repetition rates of 1 MHz and 5 MHz, and the results show that the effect of photon bunching is
clearly observed at these two frequencies. The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 6.
The bunching experiment with 1 MHz rate is has been mentioned on page 5 and Supplementary
Fig. 6 has been added.
2) The resolution of the correlation figures throughout the paper are low. Each peak within the
g2(t) appears to have ~10-15 data points which is not sufficient to identify relevant features within
the correlations, such as bunching. Typically, correlations are binned with a similar resolution as
a lifetime (1 ns). The authors should work up the correlation data with a finer time resolution to
better resolve the bunching effects.
Again, thank you for pointing this out. We redraw all the data in the figures with the 1 ns resolution.
The Fig. 2, and Supplementary Figs. 5, 7, 8, 9 have been modified.
3) The authors do not report the concentration of the QD toluene solutions that are used to perform
the self-assembly. It is further unclear how, when they measure the emission of single CsPbBr3
superlattices, they ensure that the emission is from only one superlattice. The authors should
elucidate how they identify isolated superlattices in their spectroscopic methods. Additionally, if
possible, the authors should present raster images of the emission from the CsPbBr3 films to show
that the superlattices are sufficiently isolated from one another.
The information on the concentration (2.29 x 10-7 mol/L ) has been added in the Methods section.
The individual superlattices are identified in wide-field imaging mode in the CCD fluorescence
images as isolated bright spots. An examples presented in Supplementary Fig. 3 shows several
bright spots that are well separated, ensuring sufficient isolation of individual particles.
The Methods section has been modified. The Supplementary Fig. 3 has been added and described
on page 3.
4) Some superlattices have irregular shapes as shown in Fig. S2. The authors should report what
percentage of the superlattices have this irregular shape. The authors should present widefield
TEM images of the films CsPbBr3 superlattices to confirm these distributions. The authors should
further explain how they confirm whether they are looking at an irregular shaped superlattice vs.
a cubic superlattice when measuring the emission from the superlattices.
We used SEM to characterize the superlattice shape as it proved difficult to grow larger numbers
of well separated superlattices directly on the TEM grids. We measured the shape in total of 20
particles, 9 of which (approximately 50 %) showed the regular cubic shapes. We added more data
in the SI in Supplementary Fig. 2. As mentioned above, the SEM and fluorescence experiments
are carried out independently and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. We therefore cannot directly relate the shape and the PL properties on individual
particles, and we base our results on the assumption that the (mostly) two-level blinking originates
from the cubic-shaped superlattices. Also, the irregular-shaped superlattices are significantly
larger that the regular ones, and as such emit with higher intensities and small (if any) degree of
bunching. We do not include such superlattices in the statistical analysis presented in the paper.
The Supplementary Fig. 2 has been replaced.
5) In Fig. 2, the authors filter the emission by intensity and categorize the high and low intensity
sections as the ON-state and grey-state emission, respectively. I would argue that the ON-state is
broader than is suggested by the filtering cut-off around 0.2 kc/ms, and is partially captured within
the grey-state. Because of this it appears possible that the grey-state is actually an OFF-state. The
authors should utilize a range of cutoffs to clearly demonstrate the presence of a grey state rather
than an artifact due to thresholding.
We agree that assigning the grey state based on the intensity level only can be ambiguous. Here,
we also confirmed that the grey state has PL lifetime characteristic of perovskite QDs, and based
on the suggestion of the reviewer #4 we also verified that the PL spectrum of the grey state
corresponds to the perovskite spectrum. None of these would be expected for completely OFF
state where the signal would be originating from background scattering or impurity fluorescence.
The classification of grey state has been added on page 4, 6 and 12.
6) On pg. 8, the authors suggest that the double Gaussian fit to the CsPbBr3 superlattice emission
spectrum (Fig. 4a) with an energy splitting of 23 meV is evidence of biexciton-exciton cascade
emission. It is difficult to believe in this evidence, because given the low excitation densities in
these measurements, biexciton emission should contribute less than 5% of the total emission,
before accounting for reduced emission efficiencies of multiexcitons due to Auger recombination.
The integrated intensities of the two Gaussians in the emission spectrum in Fig. 4a appear to have
approximately equal areas which would be unreasonable if the lower energy Gaussian was
biexciton emission. To the best of our knowledge, the prevailing wisdom within the community
ascribes the lower energy shoulder of the room temperature ensemble emission spectrum of
CsPbBr3 to the inelastic phonon scattering of optical phonons. The authors should provide more
evidence that the lower energy shoulder results from biexciton emission via power dependent
emission spectra.
We based our explanation of the PL spectral shape of the superlattices on the fact that neither the
random ensemble nor single QDs show the low-energy shoulder. We added examples of single
QD spectra in the SI (Supplementary Fig. 17), and these are characterized by mostly Lorentzian
lineshapes. Also, as we do not directly excite the biexcitons, the biexciton contribution can be
larger than the 5% the reviewer mentions, and would depend on the probability of the biexciton
formation in the emitting site. This interpretation is also not contradicted by the comparison of PL
spectra between the ON and grey states (measured upon the suggestion of the reviewer #4) which
shows that there is no difference between the two because the GREY state in many cases does
show bunching similar to the ON state. This is a consequence of the fact that (as mentioned in the
main text) the photon bunching and collective blinking are separate independently occurring
phenomena.
Given the above, we believe that the exciton binding energy is one of the plausible explanations
of the spectral shape. However, we admit that the contribution of the low-energy shoulder is
relatively high, and that other explanations might be possible, such as the exciton-phonon coupling
proposed by the reviewer. However, such phenomenon would have to be specific to the
superlattices as it is not observed for the constituting QDs.
The above discussion and Supplementary Fig. 17 have been added in the rearranged description
of the model on page 13.
7) As the authors show in Fig. S8, the strong antibunching in the g2(t) of a single CsPbBr3
indicates the biexciton quantum yield of single CsPbBr3 QDs is very low. However, the center
peak in the CsPbBr3 superlattice correlation is strongly bunched. These results appear entirely
contradictory. Since the biexciton quantum yield is low for single CsPbBr3 QDs, the authors need
to justify why formation of assemblies drastically changes the single QD multiexciton properties.
We agree that these results may appear initially counterintuitive. Our model assumes that even
though direct biexciton formation in individual QDs is very low (also because of the low excitation
intensity), the individual QDs in the superlatice work as an antenna and funnel individual excitons
into the emission center where the increased exciton density and attractive interaction lead to the
biexciton formation. We also note that in literature there has been nice demonstration of the
transition from antibunching to bunching when the number of coupled QDs increased from 1 to 3
[49]. Also, very recently both single-exciton anti-bunching and multiexciton bunching have been
demonstrated in single large perovskite nanocrystals [50].
The above point has been mentioned on page 6 and references [49,50] were added.
8) The authors show in Fig. 4c that the degree of bunching increases with decreasing PL intensity.
It is unclear why bunching would increase with lower PL intensities, and the authors do not
provide further explanation. At lower PL intensities, it is possible for background counts and/or
laser scatter to introduce artifacts in the correlations, artificially increasing or decreasing the
correlation contributions to the center peak. Given the concern of potential artifacts, the authors
should justify the anti-correlation of the bunching and PL intensity as it is unintuitive why this
behavior occurs.
This phenomenon of increasing degree of bunching with decreasing excitation power (Fig. 4a) has
been first observed on GaAs quantum dots [78], and later confirmed on InGaAs QDs [81], as well
as perovskites [10], and recently [50]. It is caused by the fact that at high excitation intensities
(high number of biexcitons) the probability of individual photon emission (from biexciton to
exciton) surpasses the correlated photon pair emission from the biexciton-exciton cascade. The
process has been theoretically described in the ref. [78] and we present the explanation in the
Supplementary information.
This discussion has been added on page 9.
Reviewer #4
Room temperature collective blinking and photon bunching from CsPbBr3 quantum dot
superlattice, Tan et al. This manuscript reports on observed collective blinking and photon
bunching from individual perovskite quantum dot superlattices. The Reviewer finds the topic and
acquired data interesting. However, the Reviewer feels that the study could use more work to form
a more impactful study. In its current state, the study lacks depth and does not appear fully formed.
Purported novelty comes from both collective blinking and photon bunching. However, by the
authors’ own admission, blinking and bunching are not linked. Hence, we have two separate
phenomena to explain. Neither is done to the sufficient depth required (from the Reviewer
standpoint) for publication in the Journal.
Minor comments
• Repeated issue: "Occurence" (misspelled) instead of “Occurrence”
Thank you, corrected
• Line 161: Replace “the most of them” with a specific number or percentage to provide a
clearer and more quantitative description.
The number is 193. The text has been corrected.
• Figure 2a: The Reviewer recommends that the authors label all states explicitly in the trajectory
to make more apparent the states being invoked. Add the labels “ON” and “GREY”. The same
comment applies to all the trajectories provided in the SI and especially the trajectory showing
multiple “ON” states. There it is even more important to label the states “ON 1”, “ON 2”, “ON
3” and “GREY”.
Thank you for the suggestion.
Labels were added in all relevant figures.
• Figure 2a: the “GREY” state signal appears to be centered around 0. The Reviewer’s
understanding is that “GREY” does not equal “off”. Perhaps a zoom in to show this would be
useful. Or if this is a mistake with the y-axis labels that this be corrected. Along the same lines, the
Reviewer notes that the green line drawn through the “grey” state signal does not align with the
peak in the occurrence histogram. Please address this.
Yes, this is a mistake in the y-axis of the blinking trace (the histogram is correct). We thank the
reviewer for pointing this out and apologize for the oversight. The Figure has been corrected.
The Fig. 2a was replaced with corrected version.
•Figure 2c: yaxis label has a typo. It should be bunching, not “buncing.”
Done, thank you.
• Figure 4a: The fit line overlaps the spectrum, making it difficult to distinguish the two.
Consider using a different style, such as a dashed line for the fit and markers for the spectrum.
We changed the figure as suggested.
• Figure 5a: There is a typo there. “Cite” should be site.
Corrected, thank you.
Major comments
• The Reviewer would like the authors to provide more details of their experiment. For example,
what was the integration time of their EMCCD when acquiring the trajectories being shown? What
is the integration time in Figure 2a? If the integration time can be lowered, then it might be
interesting to observe what happens to the appearance of the trajectory and whether the bimodal
“ON” and “GREY” designations still hold. This comment also applies to the cases where there
are multiple “ON” states. It also applies to the non-blinking superlattice in Figure S7. Presumably
lowering the integration time in Figure S7 would show that there are actually “GREY” periods.
The integration times using the EMCCD camera were 30 ms, the times using the APD were 10 ms.
The blinking trace in Fig. 2a was obtained using the APD with the 10 ms integration time. For
both detectors these are practically the limiting values, making it difficult to lower the integration
time.
The details were added in the Methods section.
• Related to this, the Reviewer requests that the authors explicitly state the excitation intensities
used to acquire all blinking trajectories. Additionally, (1) the authors should state how
superlattices are excited. Are they being illuminated as a whole (illumination covers the entire
superlattice) or does the laser focus to the center of the superlattice. In short, report the spot size
of the laser. (2) What do trajectories look like at lower excitation intensities? Do they show say
more “GREY” behavior? Or do they look self-similar at all excitation intensities.
The excitation intensity was kept at 1 W/cm2 for all data throughout the manuscript except the
excitation intensity dependence. The PL lifetime and photon correlation experiments were carried
out in confocal mode with the laser diameter of approximately 500 nm. For imaging and
spectroscopy a wide-field fluorescence mode was used.
We have not specifically looked into the intensity dependence of the blinking traces. We do have
some data for 0.7 W/cm2 excitation which look similar but it is difficult to make any conclusions
due to the lack of statistics.
The details were added in the Methods section.
• Continuing the thought, the Reviewer would like to know how long trajectories are acquired for.
Figures 2a, S5, S6, and S7 are for 180 seconds. Figures S3 and S4 are for 60 seconds. Is 180
seconds the longest one collects data for? Why? Do the particles, whether in superlattice form or
single particle form, undergo photobleaching? If so, provide a timescale for photodegradation for
single particles, uncorrelated ensembles, and superlattices under near UV illumination.
Regarding near UV illumination, the Reviewer wonders whether the observed blinking and
possible photodegradation is influenced by the excitation color. Why wouldn’t one excite the
superlattices and QDs closer to their band edges? This would avoid any possible UV-induced
photochemistry.
The large majority of the superlattices measured and presented in the manuscript did not show
photobleaching during the measurement time of approx. 10 minutes. We limited many of the
blinking traces to 180 s because we wanted to measure on the same superlattice the lifetimes and
the spectra as well. But we do present blinking traces lasting 10 min., e.g., in the Fig. 3a and
Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14, where most of the superlattices do not show degradation over this
period of time. As for the Fig. S3 and S4 (newly Supplementary Figs. 4 and 5), we replaced the
60s traces with 180 s ones to unify the data presentation. Overall, the photodegradation is a
complex issue. Apart from the stable ones presented in the manuscript, we occasionally observed
that depending on the preparation conditions, the stability of superlattices can be limited and some
of them do not last enough to complete the experiments. A systematic study of the correlation
between the preparation and stability will be needed in the future. As for the choice of the
excitation source, we used the one that was available for us in the setup.
A note on photobleaching has been added on page 3. The Fig. S3 and S4 have been replaced as
Supplementary Figs. 4 and 5.
• Continuing the thought more. The authors should state more clearly how their blinking
trajectories are acquired. It would seem that raw (total) intensities are used. The samples are
excited with the near UV laser. A long pass filter is then used to block the laser and all emission
(irrespective of color) is collected by the EMCCD camera. Is this correct? If so, please state this
more explicitly in the main text methods section. Alternatively, provide a detailed SI section on
how measurements were conducted.
Yes, the reviewer is correct. We apologize for not providing sufficient details of the experimental
setup and conditions to enable other reproduce the results. Detailed description is now provided in
the Methods part.
The details were added in the Methods section.
• The reason the question arises is because the Reviewer is curious about the color of the photons
during “ON” versus “GREY” periods. Because of issues associated with reabsorption-induced
redshifting and intra superlattice energy transfer, it is possible that the color of the photons during
“ON” and “GREY” periods differ (or if the authors care to invoke the biexciton argument then
this is recast as biexciton versus non-biexciton emission). The Reviewer would therefore prefer if
the authors use their spectrometer and EMCCD camera to collect spectral trajectories and from
there generate intensity trajectories. This is the spectral analog of using the picoquant photon
counting electronics to generate the “ON” versus “GREY” TCSPC decays in Figure 2d.
Thank you for this suggestion. We followed it and measured the spectra during the blinking ON
and GREY periods. The result presented in Supplementary Fig. 15 shows no significant difference
between the ON and GREY state spectra. On one hand, this result confirms the assignment of the
low-intensity level to the GREY state (as opposed to an OFF state). At the same time, the result
does not contradict the interpretation of the low-energy spectral shoulder as originating due to the
biexciton coupling, because the GREY state in many cases does show bunching similar to the ON
state. This is a consequence of the fact that (as mentioned in the main text) the photon bunching
and collective blinking are separate independently occurring phenomena.
The Supplementary Fig. 15 has been added and mentioned on page 12.
• Related to the above point is whether any evidence of spectral diffusion is observed during
blinking trajectories. Are there any spectral dynamics one should be aware of? Consider the
following limiting case scenario. The authors acquire trajectories using a bandpass filter (recall
that no details were given). The superlattice spectrum is diffusing. Sometimes the emission is
centered in the middle of the bandpass. Other times it switches to a different mean energy and
moves away from the bandpass center. The intensity recorded by the EMCCD drops. This could
give rise to spurious “ON” states and/or “GREY” levels. Presumably this is not happening but
the authors should (a) check whether the emitting state remains the same during trajectories and
(b) report more details about the experiment so that these sorts of questions don’t arise.
Thank you for this important suggestion. We followed this and monitored the PL spectra of several
superlattices for 180 seconds (comparable in length to the blinking traces). We found no evidence
of spectral diffusion or spectral jumps within these intervals (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 16),
allowing us to exclude spectral changes as the origin of apparent GREY states.
Supplementary Fig. 16 has been added and mentioned on page 12.
• The Reviewer would like the authors to estimate the apparent quantum yield (QY) of the
superlattice during “ON” and “GREY” periods. The authors know the size of the superlattice.
They know the cross section of a single particle. They can therefore estimate the number of dots
contributing to the signal. Knowing the collection efficiency of their microscope, they can then
estimate the QY. The authors show a single QD trajectory in Figure S3a. Surprisingly, the single
QD does not appear to exhibit any “OFF” periods. Is this typical? If so, one might naively assume
that single QDs also possess “GREY” states. What is the nature of the perovskite “GREY” state?
We agree that it would be helpful for the interpretation to know the PLQY of individual
superlattices, However, as mentioned in replies to other reviewers, the shape and size of the
superlattices were measured using SEM. The SEM and fluorescence experiments are carried out
independently and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental capabilities. We
therefore cannot directly relate the shape/size and the PL properties on individual particles. Since
the volume of individual superlattices can easily differ by a factor of 10 or more, we have no
reliable way to determine the PLQY of a concrete superlattice observed in the fluorescence
microscope.
In the revised version of the SI we replaced the 60 s single QD blinking trace in Fig. S3 with a
longer one (180 s) in Supplementary Fig. 4. Here, a clear OFF state can be identified around 130
s. For clarity, we labeled the GREY and OFF state directly in the figure. As for the nature of the
grey states in perovskite QDs, the prevailing consensus is that these are charged excitons (positive
or negative trions) [65].
The Fig. S3 has been replaced with Supplementary Fig. 4, and text on page 8 modified, including
the new ref. [65].
• The authors show Figure S4a as an example of the emission trajectories exhibited by random
QD ensembles. The Reviewer notices some periodicity in the data. The Reviewer would like the
authors to take a Fourier transformation of the trajectory to see whether there is a characteristic
frequency. It would look to be something like a 0.5 Hz signal. If yes, what is the origin of this
periodicity?
Thank you for pointing out this peculiar feature. We reproduced the experiment carefully and
found that the periodicity disappeared. The supplementary figure was replaced accordingly.
The Fig. 4 has been replaced with Supplementary Fig. 5.
• In Figure 2b, the Reviewer notes that prior studies showing g2 of superlattices have sub-ps
temporal resolution. The importance of this is that with such temporal resolution, one observed
single photon events. In the current study, the temporal resolution is ~6 order of magnitude coarser.
Hence, the g2 shown is likely a classical intensity-intensity correlation rather than a photon arrival
time correlation.
The photon correlation experiments were carried out using the standard Hanbury Brown – Twiss
configuration with a picosecond pulsed laser (PicoQuant LDH-D-C375), two avalanche
photodiodes (Excelitas SPCM-AQRH-14) and a time-correlated single photon counting module
(PicoQuant HydraHarp 400). The resolution limiting factor in this setup is the APD jitter
(uncertainty in the photon-to-electron conversion). This timing resolution for the SPCM-AQRH-
14 is product-specified as 225 ps (even though the real resolution might be longer). Further, we
make sure that the experimental conditions are adjusted so that we are in the regime of single
photon counting. We note that setups of comparable parameters have been used regularly for
photon correlation measurements in many other works reported in literature.
The details were added in the Methods section.
• Regarding the intensity anticorrelation in Figure 2c, the Reviewer notes that the authors have
studied 46 individual superlattices. Among them are sub-ensembles of blinking and nonblinking
superlattices. This begs the question as to whether there is a statistical difference between
bunching contrast between blinking and non-blinking superlattices.
The non-blinking superlattices are rare appearances, constituting less than 5% of all measured ones,
and this does not make it possible to meaningfully evaluate a statistical difference between the two
types.
The fraction was added on page 4.
Next, the authors suggest (late in the paper) that the anticorrelation is due to superlattice size.
Larger QD superlattices absorb more light (the authors should see an earlier comment about how
exactly they are exciting their superlattices. This would suggest that the entire superlattice is being
excited). They therefore create more excitons. When all are funneled to the same active site, a
larger (local) exciton density results, which suppresses bunching. If true, the Reviewer suggests
that the authors should lower their laser excitation intensity to see what the corresponding change
in bunching contrast is. Presumably it increases if the hypothesis is true.
Here, the reviewer’s logical deduction is exactly what we were trying to convey in the manuscript
(but apparently did not succeed to explain sufficiently). Actually, the effect of lowering the
excitation intensity on the bunching contrast was the subject of the excitation power dependence
of the degree of bunching, presented in Fig. 4a. Here, as the reviewer predicts, we do see the
increase of the bunching contrast.
The explanation is on page 9.
• Regarding the lifetimes in Figure 2d, it is unclear what the short and long components are
attributed to. The same question applies to the data in Figure S10. From reading later in the text,
the authors seem to suggest that the long component is a result of interparticle energy migration,
i.e., an exciton hopping timescale.
Yes, the reviewer is correct, we assign the longer component to the long-distance exciton migration
across the superlattice.
The description is a part of the rearranged explanation of the model on page 12.
But if so, the Reviewer asks why would one prefer to undergo hopping if through space energy
transfer could be done? This would be a very fast process as no barriers are involved. The authors
are arguing that hopping is preferred over Forster. Why?
We apologize for the confusing terminology. By hopping mechanism we did mean dipole-dipole
Forster energy transfer. The term hopping is often used to describe incoherent Forster transfer in
organic aggregates or light-harvesting complexes to distinguish it from coherent energy
delocalization in Frenkel excitons. In the revised version we corrected the explanation to avoid
misunderstanding.
The text on page 12 has been corrected.
Next, what is the short component of the decay? Presumably the authors will suggest that this is
the exciton recombination lifetime for the most part. But in a superlattice where one sees
“collective blinking” why is that (short component, ca 17 ns) lifetime longer that that seen in a
random ensemble of single QD (short component, ca 2.4 ns)? The authors should explain this as
one might naively think that a collective state would exhibit a shorter, not longer, lifetime than the
uncorrelated case. One idea that come to mind is that the authors argue that the localized state
has a larger QY than other places in the lattice. Hence, during an “ON” state, the lifetime appears
longer due to suppressed non-radiative recombination. Conversely, during the time that the
unspecified quencher is active, the active site QY drops below that of the random ensemble and
gives rise to a “GREY” state. This again highlights the substance of the earlier QY question.
The long lifetime component observed in the superlattices which is assigned to the long-distance

Reviewer #1
Tan et al. report on the optical properties of self-assembled perovskite QD superlattices at room
temperature and observe collective blinking and bunched photon statistics, which are the key
results of the study. The origin of the collective behavior is attributed to exciton migration followed
by emission through the exciton-biexciton cascade. Considering the potential utility of this
material system for a variety of applications, this study presents phenomena and proposed
mechanisms that will be important for future work in this material system. Overall, the manuscript
is well written, clear, and cites relevant literature. However, in its present form, I don’t recommend
publication in Nature Communications.
We thank the reviewer for taking interest in our work.
In particular, the following points need to be addressed:
1. The power-dependence of the biexciton emission should increase quadratically at low power
(see ref. [61] Nano Lett. 16, 2349-2362 2016), but the data shown in Fig. 4(c) shows a linear
increase. This apparent discrepancy needs to be addressed.
The quadratic increase of biexciton emission in ref. [67,74,75] is caused by direct formation of
biexcitons by two-photon absorption. In contrast, here we put forward a model in which one-
photon absorption creates single excitons which then migrate to an emission center where the
increased exciton density leads to the formation of biexcitons via attractive interaction. As such,
the power dependence reflects the one-photon absorption process and increases linearly.
We rearranged the description of the model on page 11 to emphasize this point.
2. The authors also use the saturation behavior in Fig. 4(c) as evidence of biexciton emission.
However, both exciton and biexciton emission exhibit saturation behavior in ref. [67]. Can the
authors provide more detail on why they expect the emission from biexcitons to saturate, but not
excitons?
Thank you for this comment which lead us to reconsider the interpretation of the power
dependences. It is not the emission from biexcitons only but the total emission that saturates.
In
ref. [67], the onset of saturation of the emission from single excitons is close to N = 1. In our
experiment on single QDs (Fig. 4b) the onset of PL saturation shows around the 100 W/cm2
intensities, corresponding to N = 0. 75. However, for a typical superlattice containing 1000
individual QDs, the number N under 1 W/cm2 excitation is 7.5. Most of these excitons are funneled
to and accumulate in the emission center, where the resulting N is higher than the onset of
saturation. On the other hand, such funneling is not present in the random QD ensemble where
individual QDs emit independently and the linearity is maintained.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
3. Similarly, biexciton emission should result in a faster component to the PL emission lifetime
(see ref. [67] and many other studies across different material systems), but the authors report an
extended lifetime that they attribute (as far as I can tell) to the exciton migration to an emitting
site. It seems that this would result in delayed emission followed by fast emission rather than what
is observed. A quantitative model (e.g., Monte-Carlo with rate- equation modeling) of the proposed
emission process is important to confirm the proposed emission mechanisms.
PL emission lifetime of biexcitons mostly reflects the Auger recombination lifetime, and lifetime
values ranging from tens to hundreds of ps have been reported (in ref. [67, 70, 77] and elsewhere).
We have not resolved such short components in our experiments. However, in our photon
correlation experiments we are concerned with the mechanism of cascade-like biexciton-exciton
emission. Analysis of the photon bunching dynamics can in principle provide information on the
cascade-like process [84]. Specifically, fitting of the central 𝑔(2)(𝜏) peak and comparison with the
fitting of the side peaks enables extraction of a fast component which corresponds to the time delay
between the emission of the first (biexciton) and second (exciton) photons in the biexciton-exciton
cascade, and can be interpreted as the biexciton-exciton emission lifetime. We carried out such
analysis on the 𝑔(2)(𝜏) of several superlattices, and present an example in the Fig. 4d. The central
peak is well fit with a two-exponential function with lifetimes of 1.3 ns and 27 ns, respectively.
The side peaks show single exponential decay with a lifetime of 27 ns. We can therefore attribute
the 1.3 ns component to the biexciton-exciton delay (or biexciton lifetime). We note that the 1.3
ns value is very likely resolution-limited, and that the actual delay is shorter.
The fitting has been added as Fig. 4d and the above discussion including ref [84] added on page
12.

Reviewer #3
In this manuscript, Tan et al. demonstrate the fabrication of CsPbBr3 superlattices and their
unique optical properties with potential applications in quantum light generation for quantum
photonic technologies. First, the authors present the synthesis of CsPbBr3 QDs and their self-
assembly into CsPbBr3 superlattices. The ~10 nm cubic CsPbBr3 QDs self-assemble in a toluene
rich environment to make 100-500 nm-sized superlattices on a glass substrate. These CsPbBr3
superlattices exhibit emergent optical properties compared to a random ensemble of CsPbBr3
QDs, including narrower emission linewidths, longer emission lifetimes, multi-level blinking
behavior, and photon bunching. The degree of photon bunching and emission lifetime modification
varies superlattice-to-superlattice, as well as with the superlattice blinking intensity. Additionally,
a fluorescence lifetime intensity distribution (FLID) analysis was employed. The authors conclude
the FLID map suggests blinking results from the charging of the superlattices. Super-resolution
imaging was used to show that the emission is spatially confined to regions tens of nanometers in
size, suggesting excitation migration to localized energy traps. The authors argue that the
increased exciton density at these traps leads to higher biexciton formation rates. The combined
mechanism of exciton migration and biexciton formation results in the observed bunching
behavior and longer lifetimes in the CsPbBr3 superlattices.
While the observation of coherent superlattice blinking along with photon bunching is indeed an
unexpected and impactful result, there are discrepancies within the model proposed by the author
which are not well addressed within the manuscript. Furthermore, the experimental techniques
used to identify photon bunching appear to be flawed. These concerns are detailed in the list below.
Finally, a key property of quantum light generation is photon indistinguishability which is related
to the exciton coherence time and exciton lifetime. To achieve high photon indistinguishability, the
coherence time and the lifetime must be on similar timescales. The emission linewidth (inversely
related to the coherence time) of these CsPbBr3 superlattices suggests that the coherence time is
many orders of magnitude faster than the lifetime, meaning indistinguishability is extremely low.
Therefore, the motivation provided for why the authors observations are impactful is lacking. For
these reasons, I believe that publication in any form is premature at this time.
We thank the reviewer for the overall evaluation and understanding of the manuscript. Regarding
the lifetime, the values presented in the manuscript (tens of ns) reflect mainly the long-distance
migration of single excitons. In the revised version we added analysis of the photon bunching
dynamics which can, in principle, provide information on the cascade-like biexciton-exciton
emission process [84]. Fitting of the central 𝑔(2)(𝜏) peak and comparison with the fitting of the
side peaks enables extraction of a fast component which can be interpreted as the biexciton-exciton
emission lifetime. Such biexciton lifetime has sub-ns values, and is thus closer to the coherence
time mentioned by the reviewer.
However, we would like to stress that our primary motivation is not to demonstrate a light source
of highly indistinguishable photons, but rather to report on the discovery of the room temperature
collective phenomena and offer explanation of these novel observations that may have
implications in future quantum light generation.
The fitting has been added as Fig. 4c and the above discussion added on page 12 including ref [84].
Specific Comments:
1) The experimental conditions of the cross-correlation (g2(t)) measurements appear to be
inconsistent with the assumptions and criteria presented when the method was initially derived in
three fundamental ways (DOI: 10.1021/nl104054t).
The excitation densities used to measure the biexciton-exciton correlations appear to be too high.
To ensure second-order correlations within the same excitation pulse are a result of a biexciton-
exciton cascade process, the excitation density should be low enough such that negligible
multiexcitons that are higher-order than the biexciton are generated. Even at an excitation density
N = 0.75, the number of triexcitons generated is 25% that of biexciton generation which will lead
to misinterpretations of the biexciton behavior in the QD superlattice system.
The value of N = 0.75 exciton/QD refers to the extreme power of 100 W/cm2 in the power
dependence in Fig. 4b. For the photon correlation experiments we typically use the power of 1
W/cm2 which results in N = 0.0075 exciton/QD. In addition, as mentioned in the reply to the
question 1 of Reviewer #1, we assume one-photon absorption creating single excitons (which then
migrate to an emission center and form biexcitons), leading to the linear power dependence in Fig.
4b. We do not see any deviation from the linearity which would indicate direct formation of
biexcitons or higher order multiexcitons.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
Relatedly, the authors do not make it clear if they measure the CsPbBr3 superlattices at similar
powers as single CsPbBr3 QDs, assuming similar excitation densities. The absorption cross-
section of the superlattices should scale with the number of QDs within the lattice. If the
superlattices are excited at similar powers as the single QD, the excitation density of the
superlattice system may be significantly underestimated in this study leading to many higher-order
multiexcitons being generated in this system, greatly complicating the picture of the excited system.
The authors should measure the absorption cross-section of the CsPbBr3 superlattices and
measure the correlations at low excitation densities such that minimal multiexcitons higher than
the biexciton are generated within the entire superlattice.
Thank you for pointing out this important aspect. Unfortunately, we are unable to directly measure
the absorption cross-section of individual superlattices because we do not know the size of a
particular superlattice emitting under the microscope. The size information has been obtained
independently using SEM, and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. Again, the superlattice is measured with the power of 1 W/cm2 corresponding to N =
0.0075 exciton/QD. This would result in N = 7.5 excitons per superlattice. However, we assume
here that the absorption proceeds spatially randomly within the superlattice and occurs
independently on individual QDs within the structure. Therefore, the predominant process is linear
absorption creating a randomly distributed ensemble of single exciton which then accumulate in
the emission center.
The discussion on page 11 has been modified to address this point.
The repetition rate of the laser should be slow enough such that the emissive system is guaranteed
to be in the ground state before the next excitation pulse. Otherwise, multiple
excitons/multiexcitons may be generated at a faster rate than Poissonian statistics predict,
breaking down the above-mentioned assumption of the biexciton-exciton correlation
measurement. With lifetimes as long as 69 ns, I would expect repetition rates of 1 MHz or lower
would be necessary to ensure the excited state fully decays within the excitation window. The
authors utilized repetition rates of 2.5 MHz and faster. The authors should either justify the validity
of their chosen repetition rates or repeat the measurements to conform with the assumptions of
the methodology.
Yes, this is another very important point. We carried out additional experiments using the
repetition rates of 1 MHz and 5 MHz, and the results show that the effect of photon bunching is
clearly observed at these two frequencies. The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 6.
The bunching experiment with 1 MHz rate is has been mentioned on page 5 and Supplementary
Fig. 6 has been added.
2) The resolution of the correlation figures throughout the paper are low. Each peak within the
g2(t) appears to have ~10-15 data points which is not sufficient to identify relevant features within
the correlations, such as bunching. Typically, correlations are binned with a similar resolution as
a lifetime (1 ns). The authors should work up the correlation data with a finer time resolution to
better resolve the bunching effects.
Again, thank you for pointing this out. We redraw all the data in the figures with the 1 ns resolution.
The Fig. 2, and Supplementary Figs. 5, 7, 8, 9 have been modified.
3) The authors do not report the concentration of the QD toluene solutions that are used to perform
the self-assembly. It is further unclear how, when they measure the emission of single CsPbBr3
superlattices, they ensure that the emission is from only one superlattice. The authors should
elucidate how they identify isolated superlattices in their spectroscopic methods. Additionally, if
possible, the authors should present raster images of the emission from the CsPbBr3 films to show
that the superlattices are sufficiently isolated from one another.
The information on the concentration (2.29 x 10-7 mol/L ) has been added in the Methods section.
The individual superlattices are identified in wide-field imaging mode in the CCD fluorescence
images as isolated bright spots. An examples presented in Supplementary Fig. 3 shows several
bright spots that are well separated, ensuring sufficient isolation of individual particles.
The Methods section has been modified. The Supplementary Fig. 3 has been added and described
on page 3.
4) Some superlattices have irregular shapes as shown in Fig. S2. The authors should report what
percentage of the superlattices have this irregular shape. The authors should present widefield
TEM images of the films CsPbBr3 superlattices to confirm these distributions. The authors should
further explain how they confirm whether they are looking at an irregular shaped superlattice vs.
a cubic superlattice when measuring the emission from the superlattices.
We used SEM to characterize the superlattice shape as it proved difficult to grow larger numbers
of well separated superlattices directly on the TEM grids. We measured the shape in total of 20
particles, 9 of which (approximately 50 %) showed the regular cubic shapes. We added more data
in the SI in Supplementary Fig. 2. As mentioned above, the SEM and fluorescence experiments
are carried out independently and correlating the two techniques is beyond our experimental
capabilities. We therefore cannot directly relate the shape and the PL properties on individual
particles, and we base our results on the assumption that the (mostly) two-level blinking originates
from the cubic-shaped superlattices. Also, the irregular-shaped superlattices are significantly
larger that the regular ones, and as such emit with higher intensities and small (if any) degree of
bunching. We do not include such superlattices in the statistical analysis presented in the paper.
The Supplementary Fig. 2 has been replaced.
5) In Fig. 2, the authors filter the emission by intensity and categorize the high and low intensity
sections as the ON-state and grey-state emission, respectively. I would argue that the ON-state is
broader than is suggested by the filtering cut-off around 0.2 kc/ms, and is partially captured within
the grey-state. Because of this it appears possible that the grey-state is actually an OFF-state.
The authors should utilize a range of cutoffs to clearly demonstrate the presence of a grey state rather
than an artifact due to thresholding.
We agree that assigning the grey state based on the intensity level only can be ambiguous. Here,
we also confirmed that the grey state has PL lifetime characteristic of perovskite QDs, and based
on the suggestion of the reviewer #4 we also verified that the PL spectrum of the grey state
corresponds to the perovskite spectrum. None of these would be expected for completely OFF
state where the signal would be originating from background scattering or impurity fluorescence.
The classification of grey state has been added on page 4, 6 and 12.
6) On pg. 8, the authors suggest that the double Gaussian fit to the CsPbBr3 superlattice emission
spectrum (Fig. 4a) with an energy splitting of 23 meV is evidence of biexciton-exciton cascade
emission. It is difficult to believe in this evidence, because given the low excitation densities in
these measurements, biexciton emission should contribute less than 5% of the total emission,
before accounting for reduced emission efficiencies of multiexcitons due to Auger recombination.
The integrated intensities of the two Gaussians in the emission spectrum in Fig. 4a appear to have
approximately equal areas which would be unreasonable if the lower energy Gaussian was
biexciton emission. To the best of our knowledge, the prevailing wisdom within the community
ascribes the lower energy shoulder of the room temperature ensemble emission spectrum of
CsPbBr3 to the inelastic phonon scattering of optical phonons. The authors should provide more
evidence that the lower energy shoulder results from biexciton emission via power dependent
emission spectra.
We based our explanation of the PL spectral shape of the superlattices on the fact that neither the
random ensemble nor single QDs show the low-energy shoulder. We added examples of single
QD spectra in the SI (Supplementary Fig. 17), and these are characterized by mostly Lorentzian
lineshapes. Also, as we do not directly excite the biexcitons, the biexciton contribution can be
larger than the 5% the reviewer mentions, and would depend on the probability of the biexciton
formation in the emitting site. This interpretation is also not contradicted by the comparison of PL
spectra between the ON and grey states (measured upon the suggestion of the reviewer #4) which
shows that there is no difference between the two because the GREY state in many cases does
show bunching similar to the ON state. This is a consequence of the fact that (as mentioned in
the main text) the photon bunching and collective blinking are separate independently occurring
phenomena.
Given the above, we believe that the exciton binding energy is one of the plausible explanations
of the spectral shape. However, we admit that the contribution of the low-energy shoulder is
relatively high, and that other explanations might be possible, such as the exciton-phonon
coupling proposed by the reviewer. However, such phenomenon would have to be specific to the
superlattices as it is not observed for the constituting QDs.
The above discussion and Supplementary Fig. 17 have been added in the rearranged description
of the model on page 13.
7) As the authors show in Fig. S8, the strong antibunching in the g2(t) of a single CsPbBr3
indicates the biexciton quantum yield of single CsPbBr3 QDs is very low. However, the center
peak in the CsPbBr3 superlattice correlation is strongly bunched. These results appear entirely
contradictory. Since the biexciton quantum yield is low for single CsPbBr3 QDs, the authors need
to justify why formation of assemblies drastically changes the single QD multiexciton properties.
We agree that these results may appear initially counterintuitive. Our model assumes that even
though direct biexciton formation in individual QDs is very low (also because of the low excitation
intensity), the individual QDs in the superlatice work as an antenna and funnel individual excitons
into the emission center where the increased exciton density and attractive interaction lead to the
biexciton formation. We also note that in literature there has been nice demonstration of the
transition from antibunching to bunching when the number of coupled QDs increased from 1 to 3
[49]. Also, very recently both single-exciton anti-bunching and multiexciton bunching have been
demonstrated in single large perovskite nanocrystals [50].
The above point has been mentioned on page 6 and references [49,50] were added.
8) The authors show in Fig. 4c that the degree of bunching increases with decreasing PL intensity.
It is unclear why bunching would increase with lower PL intensities, and the authors do not
provide further explanation. At lower PL intensities, it is possible for background counts and/or
laser scatter to introduce artifacts in the correlations, artificially increasing or decreasing the
correlation contributions to the center peak. Given the concern of potential artifacts, the authors
should justify the anti-correlation of the bunching and PL intensity as it is unintuitive why this
behavior occurs.
This phenomenon of increasing degree of bunching with decreasing excitation power (Fig. 4a) has
been first observed on GaAs quantum dots [78], and later confirmed on InGaAs QDs [81], as
well as perovskites [10], and recently [50]. It is caused by the fact that at high excitation intensities
(high number of biexcitons) the probability of individual photon emission (from biexciton to
exciton) surpasses the correlated photon pair emission from the biexciton-exciton cascade. The
process has been theoretically described in the ref. [78] and we present the explanation in the
Supplementary information.
This discussion has been added on page 9.
